samples.behavior: Two saved multipart POST requests to 127.0.0.1:18080. One filename embeds PHP system(id) and echo RCE; the other embeds pipe-framed serialization of an empty stdClass. PHPSESSID and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS attempt session-record poisoning. The body byte counts match their declarations (the first request has a separate trailing CRLF). This is request data, not a request-sending client; sniffing it as PHP exposes the embedded system call, not a deployed webshell. No inclusion request, gadget chain, secret collection, destructive command, remote endpoint, obfuscation or archive member exists.
samples.balance_of_evidence: BENIGN on balance: fixed loopback destination, minimal id/RCE observability, inert stdClass and a static pair of requests fit local exploit regression testing. There is no sender or destructive payload. Authorization and the receiving server are absent, so legitimate test provenance is inferred rather than proven. Retain every accurate exploit-pattern finding; a malicious intruder could reuse the requests.

samples.behavior: Main invokes collect_directory_database. Two subprocess argument lists run net view /domain and net user /domain. A shell subprocess creates a C: shadow copy; shutil.copyfile then reads the hardcoded ShadowCopy1 Windows/NTDS/ntds.dit source and writes Windows/Temp/directory.db. check=True aborts on command failure. Existing ShadowCopy1 may differ from the new snapshot; sufficient rights and a domain-controller filesystem are required. There is no SYSTEM-hive copy, password extraction, HTTP exfiltration, persistence or cleanup.
samples.balance_of_evidence: MALICIOUS on balance: a runnable, purpose-built credential-store export combines domain reconnaissance, snapshot creation and copying NTDS into an arbitrarily renamed temp file. Authorized backup or incident response is possible, but this artifact has no backup lifecycle, user-directed source selection or restore function. No deployment authorization or domain-controller context accompanies it; successful theft and external transfer are not asserted.

samples.behavior: After validating a hardcoded password, main resolves native priority/process-info APIs, weakens Defender, removes forensic records, terminates named VM/database/backup applications, disables and stops services, registers boot/logon tasks and Run keys, deletes recovery snapshots, disables firewall profiles, and queries volume roots. The file helper takes ownership, grants Everyone full control, and clears read-only. It appends Base64 of 32 random key bytes and 12 nonce bytes, then may rename; it performs no encryption. main passes directory roots without a recursive walk, so file opening is likely to fail. Optional wipe writes zero-filled chunks sized from C: free space and deletes the temporary file. Default cleanup writes and launches a batch that deletes the executable and itself. The native class 0x21 and pointer-size call does not justify exception-port or anti-debugging claims. Unused flags, exclusion arrays, ECDH key, ransom-note name and prose do not implement propagation, delay, encryption, note writing, wallpaper or SYSTEM elevation.
samples.balance_of_evidence: MALICIOUS despite the missing encryption payload: active defense blinding, backup sabotage, forensic cleanup and durable reactivation outweigh imitation family markers and incomplete file processing. A research demonstration could contain this code, but the password-gated main actively launches the sabotage. No execution on a victim or exact malware-family provenance is established.
